result:
The page is blank, which is the only honest starting place. Everything else is a negotiation with silence.

I keep thinking about how much of a life is spent arranging the furniture of attention. You move the chair of worry closer to the window so you can watch the street, then you drag the table of obligation into the center of the room so nothing else can pass, and by evening the space is so crowded you can barely turn around. Writing freely is the rare hour when you shove all of it against the walls and stand in the middle with your arms out, just to feel the air again.

Yesterday I watched a child on a sidewalk try to balance a stick on one finger. The stick kept falling. Each time he picked it up with the same unhurried seriousness, as if the universe had personally asked him to solve this small problem and he had accepted. No audience, no score, no future use for the skill. Just the stick, the finger, and the next attempt. I envied the purity of it. Most of what adults call purpose is just the stick with extra steps and a LinkedIn profile.

There is a kind of weather that only exists between deciding to begin and actually beginning. It feels like standing in a doorway with one hand on the frame, listening to two different rooms at once. In one room everything is already known and therefore safe and therefore faintly dead. In the other room the sentence you haven’t written yet is still capable of surprising you, which means it is also capable of disappointing you, which means you might have to meet yourself without the usual excuses. Most people step back into the known room and call it prudence. The ones who step forward usually discover that the disappointment is smaller than the not-knowing, and that the surprise, when it arrives, rearranges the furniture whether you invited it to or not.

So here is a small rearrangement: the light outside is the color of weak tea. Somewhere a dog is arguing with a squirrel and losing on points. The stick is still falling, and the child is still picking it up. None of this needs to become anything else. It is already enough to have noticed, and to have left a little clear space on the floor where something unplanned might land.
